section_summary: This section documents suspected Japanese espionage, sabotage planning, diplomatic communications, courier networks, and racial propaganda across Latin America, with particular attention to Peru, Mexico, Bolivia, Colombia, Panama, and Guatemala. It also records a coordinated U.S.–Chinese effort to use Chinese diplomatic officials and local Chinese communities to observe Japanese activities, producing reports from Mexico, Peru, Nicaragua, Cuba, Guatemala, and Panama. A separate sequence concerns the harmful presentation of Axis communiqués by Colombian newspapers and the State Department's debate over censorship and press freedom.

subfiles.title: ONI Report No. 94-42: Japanese military officers in Latin America
subfiles.about: Profiles Japanese military officers who traveled through Mexico and South America and were suspected of espionage, sabotage planning, and intelligence collection.
subfiles.summary: The report traces Yoshioka, Kaneko, Uchida, Waki, Kimura, Ishii, and Miyazawa from their September 1941 departure from Japan through Mexico and onward to Peru, Bolivia, and Colombia. It alleges attempts to smuggle mercury, a bombing-target map of the Panama Canal, efforts to place agents aboard Pan American aircraft and ships, and offers by Japanese officers to instruct the Peruvian military. The report concludes that several of the officers were dangerous spies and notes plans to intern Japanese officials departing Mexico.

subfiles.title: FBI laboratory report on intercepted Japanese cablegrams
subfiles.about: Reports the FBI laboratory's examination of eleven intercepted Japanese cablegrams addressed to La Paz and Lima.
subfiles.summary: One plain-language message to Yamamoto in La Paz advised withdrawing deposits to prevent their freezing and converting the funds to dollars if necessary. The remaining messages appeared to use Japanese diplomatic or enciphered codes, with cable addresses and signatures associated with Japanese embassies, legations, and consulates. The laboratory could not decode them without the relevant codebooks.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 573 transmitting cablegram analysis to La Paz
subfiles.to: American chargé d'affaires ad interim, La Paz
subfiles.about: Provides the American Legation in La Paz with the confidential findings on intercepted Japanese diplomatic telegrams.
subfiles.summary: The instruction reproduces the identifying groups of eleven intercepted messages and the FBI's interpretation of their addresses and signatures. It includes the translation of the message advising withdrawal of deposits but explains that the other messages could not be deciphered without Japanese codebooks.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese Catholic and racial propaganda
subfiles.from: Division of the American Republics, Department of State
subfiles.about: Connects Japanese anti-white racial propaganda with Catholic outreach and alleged subversive networks in the Western Hemisphere.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum discusses a Japanese Catholic friendship mission to Brazil, Japanese representation at the Vatican, and Hachiya and Company as a possible center of Japanese Catholic propaganda. It identifies Zeco or Jocko Amari as a Japanese Foreign Office adviser familiar with South America. It also notes racial agitation among Black workers in the Canal Zone and the British Caribbean, allegedly associated with Vicente Cardinali.

subfiles.title: Letter on Japanese anti-white propaganda in Latin America
subfiles.about: Warns that Japanese racial propaganda was appealing to Indigenous, mestizo, and Black populations against white rule in the Americas.
subfiles.summary: Powers describes an argument portraying Japan as the champion of racial equality and Indigenous Americans as culturally and ancestrally linked to Japan. The propaganda urged Latin American populations to expel white domination as Japan was doing in Asia and cited Japanese victories as evidence that subordinated peoples could improve their position by aiding Japan. Powers believed the message was spreading informally and dangerously through Latin America.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 624 on harmful foreign press dispatches
subfiles.about: Reports growing criticism of United Press and Havas dispatches from Tokyo, Europe, and Washington.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy states that continued publication of the dispatches was harmful to Allied interests in Colombia. It urges that every effort be made to correct the situation.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 583 requesting examples of harmful dispatches
subfiles.about: Requests samples of United Press and Havas stories that had provoked criticism in Colombia.
subfiles.summary: The Department asks the Embassy to identify individual stories so that their origin and danger can be evaluated. It states that specific examples are necessary before corrective methods can be considered.

subfiles.title: Bonsal memorandum directing a reply to Bogotá
subfiles.about: Directs follow-up action on Bogotá's complaint about United Press and Havas dispatches.
subfiles.summary: Bonsal refers to telegram No. 624 and asks Dreier to ensure that an appropriate reply is prepared. The memorandum is an internal routing and action note.

subfiles.title: Department of State transmittal of Lima despatch No. 3538
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division; Office of Naval Intelligence; Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Distributes a copy of the Lima Embassy's report on Japanese activities in Peru.
subfiles.summary: The Department forwards the strictly confidential despatch to the principal military, naval, and domestic intelligence agencies. The enclosure is identified as Lima despatch No. 3538 of April 30, 1942.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3538: Japanese Activities in Peru
subfiles.from: R. Henry Norweb, American Embassy, Lima
subfiles.about: Corrects and supplements earlier information about Japanese cover addresses and courier services in Peru and Chile.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy identifies Motozo Nonomiya and Masaki Yodokawa as users or arrangers of cover addresses and lists additional addresses associated with Shoichi Tanaka and suspected Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha agents. It reports, without corroboration, that Japanese and German couriers may have met near Iquitos and traveled along the Amazon and Ucayali Rivers to Lima. The Embassy promises continued investigation of all aspects of Japanese activity in Peru.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 1566 on Japanese cover addresses in Santiago
subfiles.about: Alerts the Santiago Embassy to an address believed to be used by Japanese agents connected with the K Line.
subfiles.summary: The instruction quotes Lima despatch No. 3538 concerning cover addresses in Lima and Santiago. It identifies Aurelio Ibarra's Avenida Santa María address and notes that the users were believed to be Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha agents.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 2747 on an alleged South American courier route
subfiles.about: Passes to the Rio Embassy an uncorroborated report of a German-Japanese courier route between Brazil and Peru.
subfiles.summary: The quoted report says Peruvian couriers met couriers from Brazil near Iquitos and traveled by the Amazon and Ucayali Rivers to Lima. It emphasizes that the account had not been corroborated and that the Lima Embassy could not vouch for its reliability.

subfiles.title: Hoover letter forwarding memorandum on the west coast of South America
subfiles.about: Forwards confidential-source information on Japanese activities along the west coast of South America.
subfiles.summary: Hoover describes the source as highly reliable and confidential. He notes that the same material was being furnished to the Coordinator of Information, the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs, and military and naval intelligence officials.

subfiles.title: Japanese Activities Along the West Coast of South America
subfiles.about: Analyzes foreign racial and social agitation among Indigenous and mestizo populations, especially in Peru, Bolivia, and Ecuador.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum traces earlier agitation to Communist, Nazi, or other foreign influences and argues that Axis propaganda was exploiting economic and racial grievances. It singles out Japanese agents in Peru and compares their methods with Japanese appeals to local populations in Southeast Asia. It also mentions a Spanish translation of an article titled “Parallel Between Japanese and Spanish Civilizations” and fears of a Japanese-inspired Indigenous uprising near Arequipa.

subfiles.title: Routing note on instructions and sealed Chinese correspondence
subfiles.about: Explains the origin of instructions concerning Chinese cooperation and suggests personal delivery of a sealed reply from Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The note states that instructions were drafted at Under Secretary Welles's request after his discussion with Dr. Soong. It advises Far Eastern Affairs, which was in contact with Soong, that it might deliver the sealed reply received from Mexico.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary's memorandum on Chinese assistance against Japanese subversion
subfiles.about: Orders preparation of instructions for using Chinese diplomats and communities to report Japanese subversive activity in the American republics.
subfiles.summary: Welles recounts his discussion with T. V. Soong, who agreed to instruct Chinese diplomatic representatives to assist local governments and the United States. Because China lacked secure communications, the United States offered to carry Soong's sealed letters in diplomatic pouches. Duggan was directed to prepare instructions for American chiefs of mission to deliver the letters and coordinate the resulting cooperation.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Rio de Janeiro on Chinese surveillance cooperation
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Directs delivery of Soong's sealed letter and coordination with Chinese and Brazilian officials on Japanese surveillance.
subfiles.summary: Caffery is asked to give the sealed instruction to the Chinese minister in Rio de Janeiro and discuss how Chinese assistance could be made effective. He may also consult the Brazilian foreign minister so that the Brazilian government can use the information quickly.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 375 to Managua on Chinese surveillance cooperation
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Directs delivery of Soong's letter to the Chinese consul general and coordination with Nicaragua on Japanese activities.
subfiles.summary: Cochran is instructed to confer with the Chinese consul general about gathering information on Japanese subversion. He is also authorized to discuss use of the Chinese assistance with Nicaragua's foreign minister.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 800 to Panama on Chinese surveillance cooperation
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Directs delivery of Soong's letter and consultation with Chinese and Panamanian officials about Japanese subversion.
subfiles.summary: Wilson is asked to hand the sealed instruction to the Chinese minister in Panama and discuss practical surveillance arrangements. He may consult the Panamanian foreign minister to facilitate the government's use of Chinese assistance.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 636 to Mexico on Chinese surveillance cooperation
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Directs the Mexico Embassy to establish cooperation with the Chinese minister concerning Japanese activities.
subfiles.summary: Messersmith is instructed to deliver Soong's sealed letter and discuss how Chinese diplomatic officials and communities could aid surveillance. He is authorized to consult the Mexican foreign minister so the Mexican government can use the resulting intelligence.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 1595 to Havana on Chinese surveillance cooperation
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Directs delivery of Soong's instruction to the Chinese minister in Havana and consultation with Cuban authorities.
subfiles.summary: Briggs is asked to discuss effective Chinese assistance in observing Japanese activities in Cuba. He is authorized to approach the Cuban minister of state so that the Cuban government can make prompt use of such intelligence.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 1469 to Santiago on Chinese surveillance cooperation
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Directs delivery of Soong's instruction to the Chinese chargé d'affaires and coordination with Chile.
subfiles.summary: Bowers is to confer with the Chinese chargé about collecting information on Japanese subversive activity. He may also consult Chile's foreign minister to arrange government use of the Chinese assistance.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 1074 to Guatemala on Chinese surveillance cooperation
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Directs delivery of Soong's instruction to the Chinese consul general in Guatemala.
subfiles.summary: Des Portes is asked to discuss with the Chinese consul general how Chinese cooperation could help monitor Japanese activities. He may consult Guatemala's foreign minister to facilitate rapid use of any resulting information.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding the Guatemalan Chinese consul's reply
subfiles.about: Forwards a letter from the Chinese consul general in Guatemala to the Chinese foreign minister.
subfiles.summary: Welles states that the communication was received through the American Legation in Guatemala. He encloses it for Soong with a brief personal covering message.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 1268 to Lima on Chinese surveillance cooperation
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Directs delivery of Soong's instruction to the Chinese minister in Lima and coordination of Chinese assistance in Peru.
subfiles.summary: Patterson is instructed to consult the Chinese minister about using diplomatic personnel and Chinese residents to observe Japanese activity. He may also discuss the plan with Peru's foreign minister to enable prompt government use of the information.

subfiles.title: Internal note on United Press reporting of the Coral Sea battle
subfiles.about: Objects to United Press transmitting a Tokyo-via-Vichy claim that the Battle of the Coral Sea was a Japanese triumph.
subfiles.summary: The note argues that unqualified transmission of the Japanese claim showed a need for action. It was routed among several Department officials concerned with Colombian press reporting.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 143: Harmful Effects of United Press and Havas Despatches
subfiles.about: Provides examples of Colombian newspaper treatment of United Press and Havas reports originating in Axis capitals.
subfiles.summary: Lane says ostensibly impartial dispatches often produced reactions unfavorable to the United States and its allies, especially when El Siglo supplied distorted headlines. He encloses clippings and contrasts El Siglo with El Tiempo's generally more accurate treatment. Colombia's war minister had noted the anomaly that Colombia sometimes had to censor stories already passed by U.S. censors.

subfiles.title: Draft instruction to Bogotá concerning El Siglo, copy 1
subfiles.about: Responds to the Bogotá Embassy's clippings by distinguishing Axis source material from El Siglo's sensational presentation.
subfiles.summary: The draft observes that most United Press stories also appeared in the New York Times but were labeled and displayed more cautiously by loyal American newspapers. It rejects suppression of enemy claims when clearly identified, arguing that blanket censorship could reduce confidence in American news agencies. It concludes that the central problem was El Siglo's headlines and prominence rather than the mere transmission of Axis communiqués.

subfiles.title: Draft instruction to Bogotá concerning El Siglo, copy 2
subfiles.about: Duplicate draft analyzing El Siglo's handling of Axis-derived United Press stories.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats the conclusion that American newspapers contextualized enemy claims while El Siglo emphasized them through headlines and placement. It argues against prohibiting publication of Axis communiqués and identifies the newspaper's editorial treatment as the principal Colombian problem.

subfiles.title: Draft instruction to Bogotá concerning El Siglo, copy 3
subfiles.about: Another duplicate of the proposed Department response on Colombian publication of Axis reports.
subfiles.summary: The draft again distinguishes the legitimate reporting of enemy claims from El Siglo's favorable and prominent presentation of them. It maintains that censorship should not suppress clearly attributed enemy communiqués and requests further Embassy comment.

subfiles.title: Concluding page of duplicate El Siglo instruction
subfiles.about: Preserves a further duplicate of the concluding paragraph of the proposed instruction to Bogotá.
subfiles.summary: The fragment states that El Siglo's treatment of the articles was the main concern. It asks the ambassador for additional comments and bears drafting initials dated August 14, 1942.

subfiles.title: Dreier memorandum explaining delay of the El Siglo instruction
subfiles.about: Explains why a June draft concerning El Siglo was held and only forwarded in August.
subfiles.summary: Dreier says he delayed his draft after learning that World Trade Intelligence was preparing an instruction about placing El Siglo on the Confidential or Proclaimed List. He was unable to obtain that instruction because it was never routed to him, so he sent his own draft forward and requested a World Trade Intelligence check.

subfiles.title: Handwritten routing note canceling the original Bogotá instruction
subfiles.about: Concludes that the originally proposed instruction to Bogotá had become unnecessary.
subfiles.summary: The note refers to communications-office material concerning censorship of news services. It states that the instruction originally intended for Bogotá now seemed completely unnecessary and asks that it be sent or returned accordingly.

subfiles.title: Howell memorandum returning the El Siglo instruction
subfiles.about: Returns the El Siglo instruction and invites review of a replacement draft.
subfiles.summary: Howell refers to a telephone conversation and returns Dreier's instruction. He says he would like to see the new instruction and agrees that repeated reliance on the freedom-of-the-press issue had become tiresome.

subfiles.title: Mexico Embassy despatch on Chinese cooperation against Japanese subversion
subfiles.about: Reports delivery of Soong's letter and creation of U.S.–Chinese liaison arrangements in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Messersmith delivered the sealed letter to Chinese Minister Chin Tien-ru and arranged for secretaries of the American Embassy and Chinese Legation to exchange information about Japanese activities. He planned further discussions about offering this cooperation to the Mexican government and enclosed the Chinese minister's sealed reply to Soong.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3790: Chinese Cooperation in the Investigation of Japanese Activities in Peru
subfiles.about: Describes a program pairing American and Chinese officials to investigate Japanese colonies in Peru.
subfiles.summary: The Chinese minister in Lima agreed to help enlist Chinese residents in districts with large Japanese populations, using a translated questionnaire to guide their observations. Emmerson and Wu made a preliminary visit to Huaral, Chancay, and Huacho, where Chinese residents expressed willingness to assist. A second investigative trip was planned for Cañete, Chincha, Nazca, Mollendo, and Arequipa.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Japanese colony in the Chancay Valley
subfiles.from: Mr. Emmerson, Auxiliary Section, American Embassy in Lima
subfiles.about: Records preliminary findings from a May 19 visit to Japanese communities in the Chancay Valley.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum estimates a Japanese population of 4,000 to 5,000, identifies Nikunatsu Okada as a prominent cotton planter, and describes operating Japanese schools and evasion of travel restrictions through bribery. Chinese interviewees distinguished mainland Japanese from Okinawans and reported Japanese fishing parties and continued access to merchandise. The author concludes that sustained guidance could make Chinese residents valuable sources on Japanese activities.

subfiles.title: Questionnaire for investigation of Japanese activities in Peru
subfiles.about: Lists standardized questions for gathering information about Japanese communities in Peru.
subfiles.summary: The questionnaire asks about population, leaders, organizations, schools, occupations, property, travel, radios, weapons, military drills, economic conditions, and contact with Japanese officials. It also seeks evidence of police supervision, reactions to expulsions, associations with Germans or Italians, and suspicious incidents.

subfiles.title: Department transmittal of Lima despatch No. 3790
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division; Office of Naval Intelligence; Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Distributes the Lima Embassy's report on Chinese assistance in investigating Japanese activities.
subfiles.summary: The Department sends copies of despatch No. 3790 and its enclosure to military, naval, and federal intelligence agencies. The transmittal identifies the report by title and date.

subfiles.title: Lima follow-up on delivery of Soong's instruction
subfiles.about: Reports delivery of Soong's letter to the Chinese minister and evaluates the practical requirements for Chinese intelligence cooperation in Peru.
subfiles.summary: Patterson delivered the instruction to Mr. Li in the presence of Emmerson, and the Chinese minister reiterated that his legation and staff were fully available. The Embassy emphasized that useful results required planning, personal visits, explanation, and follow-up rather than passive requests. Patterson and Li agreed that approaching the Peruvian government was unnecessary at that time.

subfiles.title: Managua despatch on Japanese activities in Nicaragua
subfiles.about: Reports that Chinese and American officials considered the Japanese subversive threat in Nicaragua negligible.
subfiles.summary: Chinese Consul General Zaung Teh Ing stated that Nicaragua's only two Japanese residents had been sent to the United States and that the remaining Korean resident strongly supported the United Nations. He knew of no Japanese sympathizers among the Chinese community. The Legation nevertheless arranged close collaboration with him on any future subversive activity.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 58: Sealed envelope delivered to Chinese Minister in Habana
subfiles.about: Reports Chinese cooperation in Cuba and suspicions concerning Japanese residents in Pinar del Río Province.
subfiles.summary: Chinese Minister Ti-Tsun Li agreed to cooperate but said the Chinese colony lacked members capable of translating Japanese competently. He was concerned that Japanese residents ostensibly growing watermelons in Pinar del Río could not support themselves from that production. Li had consulted Cuban Minister of Government Saladrigas and planned to accompany trusted police officers on an investigative trip.

subfiles.title: Department transmittal of Habana despatch No. 58
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division; Office of Naval Intelligence; Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Distributes the Havana Embassy's report on delivery of Soong's instruction and Chinese cooperation.
subfiles.summary: The Department forwards despatch No. 58 of June 2 to military, naval, and federal intelligence recipients. The enclosure is identified by its title concerning the Chinese minister in Havana.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding replies from Panama and Managua to Soong
subfiles.about: Forwards sealed replies from the Chinese minister in Panama and Chinese consul general in Managua.
subfiles.summary: The Department explains that the communications arrived under covering despatches from the American missions in Panama and Managua. Both were replies to earlier letters from Soong and are enclosed unopened.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2930: Japanese Subversive Activities
subfiles.about: Reports consultation with the Chinese consul general about Japanese activity in Guatemala and El Salvador.
subfiles.summary: Tchou Che-Tsien believed Japanese activity in Guatemala was unlikely because only about two Japanese nationals of little importance were thought to reside there. He nevertheless agreed to report anything suspicious and to ask trustworthy Chinese in El Salvador for information. Des Portes would share relevant Salvadoran reports with both the Department and the American minister at San Salvador.

subfiles.title: Chapin memorandum on additional Chinese replies to Soong
subfiles.about: Forwards two more sealed letters from Chinese diplomatic representatives for possible personal delivery to Soong.
subfiles.summary: Chapin notes that two additional despatches contain sealed communications addressed to the Chinese foreign minister. He suggests that Far Eastern Affairs may wish to deliver them personally.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2342: Chinese assistance and the status of Chinese in Panama
subfiles.about: Assesses possible Chinese help against Japanese espionage in Panama and describes the effects of Panama's Nationalization of Commerce Law.
subfiles.summary: Wilson and Chinese Minister Yorkson C. T. Shen agreed that removal of all Japanese nationals limited direct observation, though agents working for Japan might still be active. Shen promised to report suspicious activity and was already translating Japanese documents for G-2 and the Canal Zone censor. The despatch also details Chinese grievances under the commerce law, the obstruction of promised exemptions by Commerce Minister Ernesto Fábrega, and the reduction of Panama's Chinese population through emigration and Canal Zone employment.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2962: Japanese Subversive Activities in Guatemala
subfiles.about: Transmits a Chinese consul's dossier showing more Japanese residents in Guatemala than the Legation had previously believed.
subfiles.summary: Tchou Che-Tsien supplied a list and brief dossier on every adult in Guatemala with Japanese nationality or a claim to it. The Legation corrected some names because the underlying police spellings were unreliable and noted that the list contained ten people, at least seven more than expected. Des Portes adds that the last Japanese men in El Salvador had been deported to the United States, leaving at least one woman not believed to be subversive.

subfiles.title: Names and General Information Concerning Japanese Presently Residing in the Republic of Guatemala
subfiles.about: Lists biographical details on Japanese-born or Japanese-national residents of Guatemala.
subfiles.summary: The surviving page identifies residents including Shikae I, Kimi Nakagawa, Carlos Matsui Hagawa, Juan Tanauvia Kioto, Ichitaka José Chaiz, Francisco Santander Furusho, Gilberto Yutaka Matamoros, and Fujimoto Suematsu. Entries give ages, birthplaces, occupations, family relationships, residences, immigration dates, and, in two cases, police detention. The final entry is incomplete and continues beyond this section.
